name: Carvedilol
drug_class: Non-selective beta-blocker with alpha-1 blocking activity
route_note: oral tablet twice daily with food; extended-release capsule once daily

discovery.note: A carbazole beta-blocker with vasodilating alpha-1 blockade; licensed to SmithKline Beecham in the US. Year of first patent (1978), per Wikipedia.

tagline: Vasodilating beta-blocker that reduced mortality in heart failure
summary: Carvedilol blocks β1, β2 and α1 adrenoceptors, combining heart-rate reduction with vasodilation. It is used in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, left ventricular dysfunction after myocardial infarction and hypertension.
mechanism: Carvedilol is a racemate: the S-enantiomer blocks β1- and β2-receptors, while both enantiomers block α1-receptors, lowering peripheral vascular resistance.
In heart failure, sustained blockade of sympathetic overactivity reduces remodelling and arrhythmias. It also has antioxidant properties in laboratory studies, of uncertain clinical significance.
uses: Chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
Left ventricular dysfunction after myocardial infarction

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: Approved in the US as Coreg for hypertension.

history.title: US Carvedilol HF trials
history.detail: The US carvedilol programme shows reduced mortality in heart failure.

history.title: Heart failure indication
history.detail: Carvedilol becomes the first beta-blocker approved by the FDA for heart failure.

history.title: COPERNICUS
history.detail: Mortality is reduced in severe heart failure.

history.title: COMET
history.detail: Carvedilol reduces mortality compared with metoprolol tartrate in heart failure.

history.title: US generics
history.detail: Generic carvedilol becomes available in the US.

facts: COMET compared it with immediate-release metoprolol tartrate, not the succinate form proven in MERIT-HF, which remains a point of debate.

references.title: Packer M et al. Effect of carvedilol on survival in severe chronic heart failure (COPERNICUS). N Engl J Med 2001
